# ML-3, process side — generated by `run_process.py`, not hand-edited

The spec asks for a Tennessee-Eastman-style process case with residual-based features and the process-monitoring classics — Mahalanobis / PCA-T² / SPE — named as such. This is that half.

**It is TE-*style*, not TE.** The real Downs-and-Vogel model is a FORTRAN plant simulation with fifty states, and reimplementing it here would be a claim I could not support. This is a reactor / separator / stripper loop with the structure that matters for monitoring: variables coupled by physical relationships, plus a recycle that carries a disturbance around the loop. Every derived tag is computed *from* its drivers, so the covariance structure is a consequence of the process rather than something imposed on it — which is what makes it possible to break a relationship while leaving magnitudes in range.

## Why the process side is a different problem from the bearing side

A bearing gives one signal with physics in its **frequency content**: the fault frequencies come from geometry and you go and look at them. A process gives eighteen signals with physics in their **relationships**: pressure is a function of temperature and feed rate, level is the integral of in minus out, and no single tag tells you anything.

So on the bearing side feature engineering *is* the physics. On the process side the physics is a set of constraints between variables, and a fault is a violated constraint — which is invisible in every individual variable.

## T² and SPE, and why monitoring only T² misses the point

PCA splits the measurement space in two. The first *k* components span the **model plane** — the subspace the process normally moves in, which encodes the correlation structure. Everything orthogonal to it is the **residual space**, which under normal operation holds only noise.

| statistic | measures | reads as |
|---|---|---|
| **T²** | distance from centre, *inside* the model plane | a normal state, at an extreme magnitude |
| **SPE** (Q) | distance *from* the model plane | a state that violates the process's own relationships |

A fault that moves the operating point along the normal correlation structure raises T² and leaves SPE flat. A fault that breaks a relationship raises SPE and can leave T² flat — **and it is invisible to every univariate chart, because no single variable left its own limits.**


## Fault: `feed_composition_step`

*IDV-1 style: a step in feed A composition. The process moves to a new operating point ALONG its normal correlation structure.*

PCA kept **8 components** (91.4% of variance). Fault begins at sample 1000 of 3000.

| detector | samples to sustained detection | false alarms per 1000 pre-fault samples | alarm fraction after onset |
|---|---|---|---|
| univariate 3-sigma (the wall of charts) | **773** | 0.0 | 8% |
| PCA T2 only | **523** | 0.0 | 5% |
| PCA SPE only | **never** | 0.0 | 2% |
| T2 or SPE | **523** | 0.0 | 6% |
| residual (model-based) | **1259** | 0.0 | 4% |

**First diagnosis:** SPE fired — *relationships broken -- a state that violates the process's own correlations*. Leading contributors: `cool_water_outlet_temp`, `reactor_level`, `recycle_flow`.


## Fault: `heat_exchanger_fouling`

*IDV-4 style: cooling capacity degrades slowly. The COOLING-FLOW-to-TEMPERATURE relationship changes while both stay in range.*

PCA kept **8 components** (91.4% of variance). Fault begins at sample 1000 of 3000.

| detector | samples to sustained detection | false alarms per 1000 pre-fault samples | alarm fraction after onset |
|---|---|---|---|
| univariate 3-sigma (the wall of charts) | **773** | 0.0 | 6% |
| PCA T2 only | **never** | 0.0 | 1% |
| PCA SPE only | **1384** | 0.0 | 15% |
| T2 or SPE | **897** | 0.0 | 16% |
| residual (model-based) | **292** | 0.0 | 72% |
**And T² never fires either** — the fault does not move the process to an extreme *magnitude*, it changes which magnitudes go together. Monitoring T² alone, which is the one with the familiar name, would have missed this entirely.


**First diagnosis:** T2 fired — *normal state, extreme magnitude*. Leading contributors: `stripper_level`, `sep_temp`, `feed_a_flow`.

## Fault: `valve_stick`

*a control valve stops responding; the controller compensates elsewhere, so the loop looks stable and the relationships are wrong.*

PCA kept **8 components** (91.4% of variance). Fault begins at sample 1000 of 3000.

| detector | samples to sustained detection | false alarms per 1000 pre-fault samples | alarm fraction after onset |
|---|---|---|---|
| univariate 3-sigma (the wall of charts) | **69** | 0.0 | 53% |
| PCA T2 only | **72** | 0.0 | 44% |
| PCA SPE only | **86** | 0.0 | 11% |
| T2 or SPE | **72** | 0.0 | 45% |
| residual (model-based) | **66** | 0.0 | 59% |

T² detects 14 samples before SPE here, which is the expected ordering for a step that moves the operating point *along* the normal correlation structure — the relationships still hold, so the residual space stays quiet.


**First diagnosis:** T2 fired — *normal state, extreme magnitude*. Leading contributors: `stripper_level`, `sep_temp`, `feed_a_flow`.


## The scorecard, and it is not the one I set out to write

| fault | univariate | T² only | SPE only | residual |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `feed_composition_step` | 773 | **523** | never | 1259 |
| `heat_exchanger_fouling` | 773 | never | 1384 | **292** |
| `kinetics_drift` | never | never | never | **1259** |
| `valve_stick` | 69 | 72 | 86 | **66** |
| **fastest / missed entirely** | 0 / 1 | 1 / 2 | 0 / 2 | 3 / 0 |

**The residual model wins, and PCA does not.** residual is fastest on 3 of 4 faults, and on `kinetics_drift` it is the *only* detector that fires at all. That is not what I expected when I built this: the spec names the PCA classics and I assumed they would carry it.

**T² alone never wins once, and misses 2 of 4 faults entirely.** Which is the argument this section exists to make, arriving from the opposite direction to the one I planned: not "T² is good and SPE is better", but *monitoring T² alone is close to useless on this process*, and it is the statistic with the familiar name that everybody reaches for.

**Univariate charts are never fastest here and miss 1 of 4 outright** — but that is a consequence of how these faults were tuned, not a general law. Every one is deliberately small enough to stay inside the marginal limits, which is the regime that makes the multivariate question interesting and is also the regime univariate charts are worst in. Scale the faults up and they win everything. 
The two fail on *different* faults: univariate is fine when a fault drives a tag out of range, and structurally blind when a fault changes which values go together. **They are complements, and the case for the multivariate layer is the faults univariate cannot see rather than a general superiority.**

Note what makes that comparison fair: every fault here is tuned so that **no tag moves more than ~3 sigma from its training mean**. Larger faults make univariate charts win everything, which is what an earlier version of this simulator accidentally demonstrated — cooling-water flow moved 115 sigma and every detector fired instantly. A relationship-break argument only means anything in the regime where the marginals still look fine.


## The control: no fault

| detector | sustained alarms per 1000 samples |
|---|---|
| univariate 3-sigma (the wall of charts) | 0.0 |
| PCA T2 only | 0.0 |
| PCA SPE only | 0.0 |
| T2 or SPE | 0.0 |
| residual (model-based) | 0.0 |

Without this row the detection numbers above mean nothing — a detector that fires constantly detects everything. Limits are set at the 99th percentile of the reference data's **own** distribution rather than from a chi-squared or Jackson-Mudholkar formula, because those are exact under multivariate normality and process data is autocorrelated, mildly nonlinear and mixed across operating points. An empirical percentile carries a false-alarm rate by construction, which is the property that has to hold.

## Residual-based features, and when they are worth having

One ridge model per signal, predicting it from every other signal. If reactor temperature is normally predictable to within 0.1 °C from feed rate and cooling flow, a 2 °C residual means the relationship changed — even though 2 °C sits well inside the temperature's own control limits.

Ridge rather than ordinary least squares for a structural reason, not a numerical one: process variables are heavily collinear *by construction* — that is what makes them a process rather than eighteen independent sensors — so OLS coefficients are large and unstable, and a model whose coefficients swing between refits produces residuals that move for reasons unrelated to the plant.

| tag | R² from the other signals |
|---|---|
| reactor_press | 0.998 |
| feed_e_flow | 0.996 |
| feed_d_flow | 0.996 |
| cool_water_flow | 0.983 |
| recycle_flow | 0.979 |
| … | |
| feed_a_flow | 0.109 |
| sep_temp | 0.102 |
| stripper_temp | 0.048 |

**The R² column decides whether a residual is worth monitoring at all.** At R² = 0.05, `stripper_temp`'s residual is essentially the signal itself, and a residual chart on it is a univariate chart with extra steps. The tags at the top are the ones where a broken relationship has somewhere to show up.

## What this does not do

- **No dynamic PCA.** Process data is autocorrelated, so consecutive samples are not independent and the effective sample size behind every limit is smaller than the row count implies. Lagged copies of each variable are the standard answer and are not implemented.

- **Linear models of a nonlinear process.** Valid near the operating point they were fitted at, which is acceptable because monitoring is a local question — *has this changed* — and is exactly why the model must be refitted after a deliberate operating-point change and must **not** be refitted in response to a fault.

- **Contribution plots smear.** A fault in one variable propagates through the model into the residuals of its correlated neighbours, so the largest contributor is not always the faulty sensor. It narrows eighteen tags to two or three; an engineer still has to look.

- **It is a simulator I wrote, and that caveat is load-bearing here.** The same circularity the bearing side had before CWRU — and the bearing side is precisely where real data overturned a claim I was confident in. The relationships are the ones I built in, so a residual model that finds them has confirmed my arithmetic and nothing else. The residual model winning is exactly the result most likely to be an artefact of a generator built from linear relationships, and I would not defend it until it has been run on real TE or SKAB data.
